claims.text: Library cataloguing systematically describes and organizes library materials so that patrons and staff can easily locate them.
claims.label: the purpose of cataloguing

claims.text: Cataloguing begins with the choice of a descriptive format, most commonly the Resource Description and Access (RDA) standard.
claims.label: the RDA descriptive standard

claims.text: Catalogers examine the item itself and note its title, author, publisher, and date of publication.
claims.label: the item's recorded details

claims.text: That information is translated into a machine-readable bibliographic record, typically with software such as Koha or OCLC Connexion.
claims.label: the machine-readable record

claims.text: Catalogers assign subject headings from controlled vocabularies such as the Library of Congress Subject Headings or the Dewey Decimal System.
claims.label: the assigned subject headings

claims.text: Each item is given a unique identifier: an ISSN for periodicals or an ISBN for books.
claims.label: the ISSN and ISBN identifiers

claims.text: Catalogers also write a concise abstract or description giving a brief overview of the item's content and significance.
claims.label: the concise abstract
